SEC-MALJS-002.impact: Any external script has complete access to your page's DOM, form input (including passwords), cookies, and can perform any action the user can. A compromised external CDN or malicious script injection results in immediate data theft for all visitors.
SEC-MALJS-002.remediation:
1. Audit all external scripts being loaded:
   View page source → list all <script src="http...">
   Verify each against your list of intentionally included third-party services

2. Implement Subresource Integrity (SRI) for external scripts:
   <!-- Generated at: https://www.srihash.org/ -->
   <script src="https://cdn.example.com/script.js"
     integrity="sha384-..."
     crossorigin="anonymous"></script>
   SRI prevents script execution if the CDN delivers tampered content

3. Implement a strict Content Security Policy:
   Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self' https://allowed-cdn.com;
   Blocks any script source not explicitly listed

4. Remove any scripts you did not intentionally add:
   Check for injected wp_enqueue_script calls in functions.php
   Check all active plugins for unexpected external script loading

5. Monitor with a WAF that alerts on new external resource additions

SEC-MINER-001.title: Cryptominer Script Detected
SEC-MINER-001.description: The page loads or references a known cryptocurrency mining library (Coinhive, CryptoNight, webminerpool, minero.cc, etc.) that uses visitor browser CPU power to mine cryptocurrency without the visitor's knowledge or consent.
SEC-MINER-001.impact: All site visitors have their browser CPU hijacked for cryptomining, causing significant performance degradation, battery drain, and overheating. This is an illegal practice in most jurisdictions (Computer Misuse Act / CFAA) and results in Google Safe Browsing flagging and browser extensions blocking the site.
SEC-MINER-001.remediation:
ACTIVE COMPROMISE — remove immediately:

1. Find the miner script:
   grep -r 'coinhive\|cryptonight\|webminerpool\|minero\|coin-hive\|miner\.' \
     /var/www/html/ --include='*.php' --include='*.js' --include='*.html'

2. Check WordPress database:
   SELECT option_name, option_value FROM wp_options
   WHERE option_value LIKE '%coinhive%' OR option_value LIKE '%miner%';

3. Remove the miner code and run full malware scan (Wordfence)

4. Change all passwords after cleanup (the miner was installed by an attacker)

5. Implement CSP to prevent future injection:
   Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self' 'nonce-RANDOM';
   This blocks any script not explicitly nonce-approved

6. Report to relevant authorities if applicable

7. After cleanup, check Google Search Console for Safe Browsing alerts and request review

SEC-PORT-001.title: Database or Critical Service Port Exposed to Internet
SEC-PORT-001.description: A critical service port is accessible from the internet: database servers (MySQL 3306, PostgreSQL 5432, MongoDB 27017, Redis 6379), remote access (RDP 3389, VNC 5900), or known backdoor/reverse-shell ports (4444, 1337, 31337, 8888).
SEC-PORT-001.impact: Direct internet exposure of database ports allows brute-force attacks, exploitation of database-specific CVEs, and unauthenticated access if default credentials are in use. Backdoor ports indicate an active reverse shell listener — the server is likely already compromised.
SEC-PORT-001.remediation:
CLOSE THESE PORTS IMMEDIATELY:

1. Firewall all non-HTTP/HTTPS ports from internet access:
   # UFW (Ubuntu):
   ufw default deny incoming
   ufw allow 22/tcp  # SSH — restrict to your IP if possible
   ufw allow 80/tcp
   ufw allow 443/tcp
   ufw enable

2. iptables — block database ports from external access:
   iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 3306 ! -s 127.0.0.1 -j DROP
   iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 5432 ! -s 127.0.0.1 -j DROP
   iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 27017 -j DROP
   iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 6379 -j DROP

3. MySQL — bind to localhost only:
   # /etc/mysql/mysql.conf.d/mysqld.cnf:
   bind-address = 127.0.0.1

4. Redis — bind to localhost:
   # /etc/redis/redis.conf:
   bind 127.0.0.1
   requirepass YOUR_STRONG_PASSWORD

5. If backdoor ports are open (4444, 1337, 31337):
   lsof -i :4444  # Find what process is listening
   netstat -tlnp | grep 4444
   The server is likely compromised — perform full incident response

SEC-PORT-002.title: Admin Panel or Non-Standard Service Port Exposed
SEC-PORT-002.description: Admin panel ports (cPanel 2082/2083, Plesk 8443, Webmin 10000, phpMyAdmin 7080) or non-standard service ports are internet-accessible, providing attack surface for brute force and exploitation.
SEC-PORT-002.impact: Exposed admin panels allow unlimited brute-force attacks against hosting control panels. A compromised cPanel gives an attacker full control over all hosted sites, databases, email, and DNS.
SEC-PORT-002.remediation:
Restrict admin panel access to known IPs only:

1. UFW — allow admin ports only from your IP:
   ufw allow from YOUR_IP to any port 2082
   ufw allow from YOUR_IP to any port 2083
   ufw allow from YOUR_IP to any port 8443
   ufw deny 2082
   ufw deny 2083

2. cPanel WHM Host Access Control:
   WHM > Security Center > Host Access Control
   Deny all by default, allow only your IP

3. Use Cloudflare Tunnel or Tailscale to access admin panels without exposing ports:
   cloudflared tunnel create admin-access

4. Enable 2FA on all admin panels:
   cPanel: Two-Factor Authentication under Security

5. Disable unused services:
   service webmin stop && systemctl disable webmin

SEC-SHELL-001.title: Known Webshell Path Accessible
SEC-SHELL-001.description: A URL matching a known webshell path (c99.php, r57.php, wso.php, alfa.php, shell.php, cmd.php, etc.) returned a non-404 response. This is a near-certain indicator of an installed webshell giving attackers remote command execution.
SEC-SHELL-001.impact: CRITICAL: An active webshell gives an attacker a persistent backdoor with full server command execution capabilities — read/write any file, execute system commands, pivot to other internal servers, exfiltrate all data, and install further malware.
SEC-SHELL-001.remediation:
INCIDENT RESPONSE — treat as active compromise:

1. IMMEDIATELY block web access to the shell and take it offline:
   mv /var/www/html/shell.php /tmp/shell.php.bak
   Or block it via nginx/Apache rule while you investigate

2. Preserve evidence before deleting:
   cp /var/www/html/shell.php /tmp/evidence_$(date +%s).php

3. Find all similar files:
   find /var/www/html -name '*.php' | xargs grep -l 'eval.*base64_decode\|system.*_GET\|passthru\|shell_exec' 2>/dev/null

4. Check server access logs for shell usage:
   grep 'shell.php\|cmd.php\|r57.php\|c99.php' /var/log/nginx/access.log
   Look for POST requests — this is how shells are typically controlled

5. Determine attacker's entry point:
   - Check upload script vulnerabilities
   - Check FTP logs for unauthorized uploads
   - Check for exploited plugins (file manager, Upload plugins)

6. Rotate ALL credentials, check for new admin users, check for cron backdoors:
   crontab -l && crontab -u www-data -l
   SELECT * FROM wp_users WHERE user_registered > DATE_SUB(NOW(), INTERVAL 30 DAY);

7. Consider engaging a security incident response professional

SEC-THREAT-001.title: Server IP or Domain Listed on Threat Intelligence Blocklists
SEC-THREAT-001.description: The server's IP address is listed on Spamhaus ZEN (spam/malware blocklist) or the domain is listed on Spamhaus DBL (domain blocklist), indicating the server has been used to send spam, host malware, or is associated with botnet activity.
SEC-THREAT-001.impact: Blocklist listing causes: email delivery failures (all outbound email is rejected or spam-filtered), browser security warnings, and reputation damage. It is also a strong indicator that the server has been or currently is compromised.
SEC-THREAT-001.remediation:
1. Check exactly which blocklists you're on:
   https://mxtoolbox.com/blacklists.aspx
   https://www.spamhaus.org/lookup/

2. Identify why you were listed:
   - Spamhaus ZEN: your IP sent spam (compromised site sending email)
   - Spamhaus DBL: your domain hosted malware or phishing pages

3. Clean the compromise:
   - Scan for malware/backdoors: Wordfence full scan
   - Check PHP mail() abuse: grep -r 'mail(' /var/www/html/ | grep -v '.php#'
   - Check cron jobs for spam scripts: crontab -l && crontab -u www-data -l

4. Request delisting after cleaning:
   https://www.spamhaus.org/delist/
   Provide evidence of cleanup — most delistings happen within 24 hours

5. Prevent future spam from your server:
   # Disable PHP mail() via php.ini:
   sendmail_path = /bin/false
   # Instead, use authenticated SMTP (SendGrid, Mailgun, SES)

SEC-THREAT-002.title: Suspicious Reverse DNS — IP Resolves to Unrelated or Suspicious Host
SEC-THREAT-002.description: The server's IP address reverse-resolves (PTR record) to a hostname that does not match the target domain — indicating shared/bulletproof hosting, a recently migrated IP, or an IP assigned to a potentially malicious hosting provider.
SEC-THREAT-002.impact: Reverse DNS mismatch reduces email deliverability. Resolving to a bulletproof hosting provider indicates the infrastructure may be intentionally chosen to avoid takedown of malicious activity.
SEC-THREAT-002.remediation:
1. Check current reverse DNS:
   dig -x $(dig +short yourdomain.com) +short

2. Set correct PTR record:
   - On dedicated hosting: ask your host to create a PTR record pointing to yourdomain.com
   - On cloud (AWS EC2): use an Elastic IP and set reverse DNS in the AWS console
   - On Linode/DigitalOcean: set hostname in droplet/linode settings to match your domain

3. Good PTR format: mail.yourdomain.com → points back to yourdomain.com

4. If currently on bulletproof hosting:
   Consider migrating to legitimate hosting infrastructure
   This will also improve email deliverability and SEO trust signals

SEC-THREAT-003.title: Domain Flagged by Google Safe Browsing
SEC-THREAT-003.description: Google Safe Browsing has flagged this domain as hosting malware, phishing content, or unwanted software. This results in browser warnings for all visitors using Chrome, Firefox, and Safari.
SEC-THREAT-003.impact: CRITICAL: All major browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari) display a full-page red warning blocking visitors from accessing the site. This effectively takes the site offline for most users and causes immediate loss of traffic, trust, and revenue.
SEC-THREAT-003.remediation:
URGENT — this is an active block affecting all visitors:

1. Verify the flag:
   https://transparencyreport.google.com/safe-browsing/search?url=yourdomain.com
   Note the specific threat type (malware/phishing/unwanted software)

2. Clean the compromise (see relevant remediation based on threat type):
   - Malware: Wordfence scan, file integrity check, malware removal
   - Phishing: Remove phishing pages, check for injected content
   - Unwanted software: Remove aggressive ad scripts, deceptive downloads

3. Request Google review after cleanup:
   Google Search Console > Security & Manual Actions > Security Issues
   Click 'Request Review' after verifying cleanup is complete
   Review typically takes 1-3 days

4. Monitor with Google Search Console to receive future alerts immediately

5. Implement a WAF to prevent future compromise

SEC-TLS-004.title: HSTS Header Missing or Disabled
SEC-TLS-004.description: The Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) header is absent or has max-age=0, meaning browsers are not instructed to always use HTTPS. This leaves the site vulnerable to SSL stripping attacks on first visit and on unsecured networks.
SEC-TLS-004.impact: Without HSTS, an attacker on the same network (coffee shop, airport WiFi) can perform an SSL strip attack: intercepting the first HTTP request before the browser upgrades to HTTPS, allowing full MITM of all traffic including credentials.
SEC-TLS-004.remediation:
Add HSTS header to all HTTPS responses:

Nginx:
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    add_header Strict-Transport-Security 'max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload' always;
}

Apache:
# httpd.conf or .htaccess (inside VirtualHost for port 443):
Header always set Strict-Transport-Security 'max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload'

WordPress (via Nginx/Apache as above, not via PHP)

Verify:
curl -I https://yourdomain.com | grep -i strict

Optional: HSTS preloading (permanent):
1. Ensure max-age=31536000, includeSubDomains, preload are set
2. Submit at: https://hstspreload.org/
3. WARNING: Once preloaded, removing HTTPS breaks the site in Chrome/Firefox — only preload if you are committed to HTTPS permanently

SEC-WPCONF-001.title: wp-config.php or WordPress Config File Accessible from Web
SEC-WPCONF-001.description: WordPress configuration files (wp-config.php, wp-config.php.bak, wp-config-sample.php, .wp-config.php.swp) are accessible via HTTP, potentially exposing database credentials, security keys, and table prefixes.
SEC-WPCONF-001.impact: CRITICAL: wp-config.php contains the database hostname, name, username, and password. With these credentials an attacker can access the entire WordPress database directly, extract all content and user password hashes, inject malware, or create new admin accounts.
SEC-WPCONF-001.remediation:
1. Block direct web access to config files (should work by default in WordPress):
   # Add to .htaccess (Apache):
   <files wp-config.php>
       order allow,deny
       deny from all
   </files>

2. Delete backup copies:
   rm /var/www/html/wp-config.php.bak
   rm /var/www/html/wp-config.php.old

3. Move wp-config.php one directory ABOVE the web root:
   mv /var/www/html/wp-config.php /var/www/wp-config.php
   WordPress automatically looks one level up

4. Set strict file permissions:
   chmod 400 /var/www/wp-config.php
   chown www-data:www-data /var/www/wp-config.php

5. If credentials were exposed, rotate immediately:
   ALTER USER 'wpuser'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'new-strong-password';
   Update DB_PASSWORD in wp-config.php
   Generate new security keys: https://api.wordpress.org/secret-key/1.1/salt/

6. Check for new admin accounts and review server access logs for DB connection attempts from external IPs

SEC-WPDEBUG-001.title: WordPress Debug Mode Active — PHP Errors Exposed
SEC-WPDEBUG-001.description: WP_DEBUG is enabled and PHP errors are being displayed on-page, or the Query Monitor plugin is active and exposing database queries and performance data to unauthenticated visitors.
SEC-WPDEBUG-001.impact: Debug output exposes: full filesystem paths, PHP version details, database query structure (aids SQL injection), plugin names and versions, and internal application logic. This is a complete application information disclosure.

SEC-WPDEBUG-002.title: WordPress debug.log or Error Log Accessible from Web
SEC-WPDEBUG-002.description: The debug.log file (created by WP_DEBUG_LOG=true) or a PHP/server error log is accessible via HTTP. These logs contain PHP error messages with full filesystem paths, database query details, plugin names, and sometimes partial credentials.
SEC-WPDEBUG-002.impact: Error logs reveal: absolute filesystem paths (enabling path traversal attacks), database error details (enabling SQL injection refinement), plugin names/versions (enabling targeted CVE exploitation), and internal application state.
SEC-WPDEBUG-002.remediation:
Block web access to log files immediately:

1. Quick block via .htaccess in wp-content/:
   <Files debug.log>
       Order allow,deny
       Deny from all
   </Files>

2. Nginx — block log file access:
   location ~* /(debug\.log|error_log|.*\.log)$ {
       deny all;
       return 404;
   }

3. Disable debug logging on production:
   # wp-config.php:
   define('WP_DEBUG', false);
   define('WP_DEBUG_LOG', false);

4. Delete existing debug.log:
   rm /var/www/html/wp-content/debug.log

5. If you need logs, redirect PHP errors to a non-web-accessible path:
   # php.ini:
   error_log = /var/log/php_errors.log
   # (not inside web root)

SEC-WPPLUGIN-001.title: Known Vulnerable WordPress Plugin Version Detected
SEC-WPPLUGIN-001.description: A WordPress plugin with a known CVE or security vulnerability has been identified via its readme.txt version number. This includes plugins with critical unpatched vulnerabilities in the currently installed version.
SEC-WPPLUGIN-001.impact: Vulnerable plugins are the #1 cause of WordPress compromises. A single unpatched plugin with a publicly known exploit allows an attacker to achieve Remote Code Execution, SQL injection, authentication bypass, or privilege escalation — often with fully automated exploits available.
SEC-WPPLUGIN-001.remediation:
UPDATE ALL PLUGINS IMMEDIATELY:

1. Update via WordPress Dashboard:
   Dashboard > Plugins > Available Updates > Update All

2. Update via WP-CLI:
   wp plugin update --all

3. Check for known vulnerabilities:
   https://wpscan.com/plugins — search your plugin name
   https://patchstack.com/database — comprehensive WP vuln database

4. For plugins with no available fix:
   - Deactivate and delete the plugin
   - Find an alternative maintained plugin

5. Enable auto-updates for security releases:
   # wp-config.php:
   add_filter('auto_update_plugin', '__return_true');

6. Subscribe to WPScan vulnerability notifications:
   https://wpscan.com/api — free tier includes vulnerability alerts

7. Consider Patchstack or Wordfence for virtual patching — blocks exploits even before you update

SEC-WPPLUGIN-002.title: WordPress Plugin Directory Listing Enabled
SEC-WPPLUGIN-002.description: Directory listing is enabled on the WordPress plugins directory (/wp-content/plugins/), allowing attackers to enumerate all installed plugins and their exact versions without guessing.
SEC-WPPLUGIN-002.impact: Directory listing reveals the complete list of installed plugins with version numbers, enabling targeted attacks against known-vulnerable versions. Without listing, attackers must probe plugin paths individually — a significant additional hurdle.
SEC-WPPLUGIN-002.remediation:
Disable directory listing:

Apache — global disable:
# httpd.conf or .htaccess:
Options -Indexes

# Or in VirtualHost:
<Directory /var/www/html>
    Options -Indexes
</Directory>

Nginx — directory listing is off by default.
Verify nginx.conf does NOT contain: autoindex on;

Add an empty index.html to plugin directory:
touch /var/www/html/wp-content/plugins/index.html
touch /var/www/html/wp-content/themes/index.html
touch /var/www/html/wp-content/uploads/index.html
(WordPress core does this by default, but custom installs may not)

SEC-WPUSR-001.title: WordPress REST API Exposes User List
SEC-WPUSR-001.description: The WordPress REST API endpoint /wp-json/wp/v2/users returns a list of all user accounts including usernames, display names, and user IDs without authentication. This directly provides attacker-ready username lists for brute force attacks.
SEC-WPUSR-001.impact: All WordPress usernames are exposed in plain JSON. Attackers combine this with brute force or credential stuffing tools to systematically attempt to compromise accounts. Admin usernames are the most valuable — if 'admin' is a username, attacks focus there first.

SEC-WPUSR-002.title: WordPress Username Enumeration via Author Archives
SEC-WPUSR-002.description: WordPress author archive URLs (/?author=1, /?author=2) redirect to URLs containing the username (e.g., /author/admin/). An attacker can iterate author IDs to enumerate all usernames on the site.
SEC-WPUSR-002.impact: All WordPress usernames are enumerable via sequential HTTP requests requiring no authentication, providing attacker-ready username lists for credential attacks.

SEC-WPUSR-003.title: WordPress Login Error Messages Reveal Valid Usernames
SEC-WPUSR-003.description: The WordPress login page returns different error messages for invalid usernames ('Invalid username') versus invalid passwords ('Incorrect password'), allowing attackers to confirm which usernames exist on the system.
SEC-WPUSR-003.impact: Attackers can use binary search to identify all valid usernames with minimal requests, then focus credential attacks exclusively on confirmed accounts — dramatically improving attack efficiency.

SEC-WPVER-001.title: WordPress Version Is End-of-Life or Critically Outdated
SEC-WPVER-001.description: The installed WordPress version is end-of-life or significantly outdated. End-of-life WordPress versions no longer receive security patches, leaving the site permanently vulnerable to all publicly known exploits for that version.
SEC-WPVER-001.impact: EOL WordPress versions have numerous known, unpatched CVEs with public exploit code. Automated scanners continuously probe for outdated WordPress installs and will exploit them without manual attacker involvement.
SEC-WPVER-001.remediation:
UPDATE WORDPRESS IMMEDIATELY:

1. Via WordPress Dashboard (recommended):
   Dashboard > Updates > Update to WordPress X.X.X
   BACK UP FIRST: Dashboard > Tools > Export, or use UpdraftPlus

2. Via WP-CLI:
   wp db export backup_$(date +%Y%m%d).sql  # backup database first
   wp core update
   wp core update-db

3. Before updating in production, test on staging:
   Theme/plugin compatibility should be verified first

4. Enable auto-updates for minor security releases:
   # wp-config.php:
   define('WP_AUTO_UPDATE_CORE', 'minor'); // Updates 6.x.y automatically
   // Or for all updates:
   define('WP_AUTO_UPDATE_CORE', true);

5. Current WordPress version: https://wordpress.org/download/releases/
   Check EOL status: https://endoflife.date/wordpress

SEC-WPVER-002.title: WordPress Version Publicly Disclosed
SEC-WPVER-002.description: The WordPress version number is visible in the generator meta tag, feed links, readme.html, or wp-includes/version.php HTTP response. This aids targeted exploitation by allowing attackers to immediately identify applicable CVEs.
SEC-WPVER-002.impact: Version disclosure alone is not exploitable but significantly accelerates targeted attacks — attackers can query vulnerability databases for the exact version and skip the probing phase.

SEC-XMLRPC-001.title: XML-RPC Interface Active and Responding
SEC-XMLRPC-001.description: WordPress's xmlrpc.php endpoint is active and responding to method calls. XML-RPC is a legacy remote publishing API that is widely exploited for brute force attacks (bypassing login rate limiting), SSRF, and DDoS amplification.
SEC-XMLRPC-001.impact: XML-RPC bypasses login rate limiting plugins — an attacker can attempt thousands of credentials in a single HTTP request using system.multicall. It also enables SSRF via pingback.ping and can be used to amplify DDoS attacks against third-party targets.

SEC-XMLRPC-002.title: XML-RPC system.multicall Enabled — Brute Force Amplification
SEC-XMLRPC-002.description: The XML-RPC system.multicall method is available and allows batching hundreds of method calls in a single HTTP request. This is actively exploited to perform thousands of login attempts while bypassing rate-limiting plugins that only count HTTP requests.
SEC-XMLRPC-002.impact: CRITICAL: An attacker can test 500+ username/password combinations in a single HTTP request, completely bypassing lockout and rate-limiting controls. This makes brute force attacks against WordPress effectively unlimited even with login protection plugins.

SEC-XMLRPC-003.title: XML-RPC pingback.ping Available — SSRF and DDoS Amplification Risk
SEC-XMLRPC-003.description: The pingback.ping XML-RPC method is active. This allows any external party to use your server as a proxy to send HTTP requests to arbitrary third-party URLs (Server-Side Request Forgery) and can be used to DDoS third-party targets using your server's bandwidth.
SEC-XMLRPC-003.impact: Your server can be weaponized to: scan internal network hosts (SSRF), probe private cloud metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254), and participate in large-scale DDoS attacks against third-party targets — potentially leading to your server's IP being blocklisted and legal liability.
